title: A cloud cutover built from failure gates
dek: The staging outage, migration preflight, secret scans, and blocker register that turned a cloud move into a sequence of testable gates.
body:
I wanted the cloud cutover to be boring. The useful kind of boring: every dependency named, every failure visible, and every operator step backed by evidence before production traffic moved.

The work did not begin that way.

The first major change consolidated four staging services onto one machine. It reduced the platform footprint, but it also made the tradeoff explicit: the services now share fate. If the router fails, all four disappear together. If one process leaks memory, the rest share the pressure. That design only works when the health check reports the children rather than the container around them, and when the rollback path is written before the cutover.

Then staging went down.

The router never bound its port. One configuration limit could not hold the longer service names. A second setting tried to open a logging device that did not exist under the process supervisor. Either fault was enough to stop the router, so the shared-fate design took every service down with it.

The repair was concrete: raise the server-name limit, log through inherited streams, and add tests for both conditions. Staging recovered after the running machine was patched, then the durable fix landed with the failure modes documented. The outage gave the consolidation work something a diagram could not: proof of how the system failed under its real process model.

The next gate moved closer to the data. A service can start cleanly while its database is still missing a migration or an expected table. That produces a bad middle state: the process looks alive, requests arrive, and users get errors from a schema the application assumed was ready.

The startup path now applies pending migrations and checks the expected schema before serving requests. A follow-up caught another edge case in the development migration helper: the database tooling could be installed at the repository root while the helper only looked beside the service. The helper now recognises either location instead of reinstalling dependencies and changing the lockfile.

The security gate widened too. Scanning only the latest change misses a secret that already sits in the tracked tree. Scanning only the tree misses a credential that was removed from the latest version but remains in published history. The repository now scans the whole tracked tree at the merge gate and runs a separate scheduled history scan.

That work reviewed every finding instead of hiding noisy directories behind a broad exception. It also used a synthetic canary to prove that a secret outside the change range still fails the merge gate. The synthetic case tests the claimed scope against a path designed to escape the old one.

Finally, the production-blocker register became executable evidence rather than a checklist that could drift. It now cross-checks the hostnames and cloud project identifiers an operator would use during the cutover. That check found a real mismatch: two documented production targets named projects that did not exist, while the live staging domains belonged to different projects. The register records the discrepancy and the decision needed to resolve it instead of quietly picking one side.

Production DNS, certificates, environment promotion, and live verification still have owner actions attached to them. The register keeps that unfinished work visible.

This sequence changed how I think about readiness. The staging outage produced router invariants. The schema risk produced a startup preflight. The secret-scan gap produced wider scan scopes and a negative control. The documentation mismatch produced a contract check. Each failure or ambiguity became a gate that can fail before production traffic does.
